title: Randomized source cues and separate sharing and belief measures
why: Fixes the design and measurement causes. Randomizing source cues turns the descriptive trust and tie contrasts into causal effects. Rating sharing and accuracy separately on 1–7 scales lets the two outcomes diverge.

power_target.basis: Observed trust effect of 0.057 (H5) and MDE of 0.051 for Trust: high vs Trust: low. About 1,000 per cell gives an MDE near 0.05 on a 0/1 outcome; closer to 1,300 per cell is needed for the tie effect of 0.03 under clustering.

rationale: The source study found misinformation lowered sharing by 18.2 points and plausibility by 18.6 points, so the two moved together. High trust (+5.7) and close tie (+3.0) were associated with more sharing, but sharer attributes were not randomized and both outcomes were forced choices. Randomizing source cues and rating sharing and accuracy separately lets the two outcomes diverge.
contribution: Tests causally whether source trust and tie strength shift sharing intent more than perceived accuracy of a false headline.
hypothesis: Source trust and tie strength raise sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, especially for the false headline.
primary_outcome: Sharing intent (1-7) minus perceived accuracy (1-7, standardized), and each rating separately.
comparison: High vs low trust and close vs distant tie, on sharing versus accuracy, by headline type.
unresolved: Actual image files for the three headlines

title: Replication across populations and languages
why: Fixes the sample cause. The original shows a smaller penalty among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), but only within a Latino sample.

power_target.basis: The language gap is 0.057 (−0.201 vs −0.144), with SEs near 0.014–0.020. About 1,500 per group-by-arm cell gives an MDE near 0.04.

rationale: The source found a misinformation sharing penalty of −18.2 points and a fact-check penalty of −13.3 points, but only among US Latino adults. The penalty looked smaller among Spanish-language respondents (−14.4 vs −20.1), and that gap is confounded with sample. This design runs the same headline-type randomization in white, Black and Latino adults, with Latino adults split by survey language.
contribution: Tests whether the information-type penalty and the trust gradient generalize across racial/ethnic groups and survey languages.
hypothesis: The misinformation sharing penalty is negative in all groups, and it is smaller among Spanish-language Latino respondents than among English-language Latino respondents. High sharer trust is associated with more sharing in all groups.
primary_outcome: Chosen to share (1 if the headline was chosen in 'Which post would you be more likely to share?')
comparison: Misinformation vs true/neutral headline, with the information-type by group and by language interaction tested. The fact-check vs true/neutral contrast is secondary.
unresolved: The actual headline pairs (17 topics) and their Spanish translations must be supplied by the research team to replace the cond_note text.
Compensation, IRB number and the panel quotas must be set by the research team.
label: Generalizability

title: Belief-driven versus identity-driven sharing of misinformation
why: Fixes the missing_moderator and design causes. Randomizing source ideology and measuring both outcomes lets sharing diverge from belief when sources are co-partisan, which the original could not test.

power_target.basis: Moderator contrasts of about 0.055 (S3) with SEs near 0.017; the sharer ideology effect of 0.019 (H4) is smaller, so a cell of 1,500 targets an interaction MDE near 0.04.

rationale: The source found misinformation lowered sharing by 18.2 points and plausibility by 18.6 points, so the two moved together. Sharer ideology was not randomized (moderate sharer −1.9 points, p=0.034), and both outcomes were forced choices, so the source could not test whether source ideology pulls sharing away from plausibility. This design randomizes source ideology and measures both outcomes on separate scales.
contribution: Tests whether source ideology shifts sharing intent more than perceived accuracy, which separates belief-driven from identity-driven sharing.
hypothesis: If sharing follows belief, the source effect on sharing equals its effect on accuracy. If identity drives sharing, the co-ideological source effect on sharing exceeds its effect on accuracy, especially for false headlines and among respondents in the top tertile of belief in disputed claims.
primary_outcome: Difference between sharing intent and accuracy rating (both standardized), by source condition, headline veracity and belief tertile.
comparison: Co-ideological versus opposed and neutral source; outcome (share vs accuracy) by source interaction, moderated by belief tertile and headline veracity.
unresolved: The actual headline texts and outlet names must be supplied and pretested for veracity and topic salience.
IRB approval number and compensation must be supplied by the research team.
